title: Body-Brain Connections
coreMove: Trauma keeps physiology organized for defense; recovery starts by restoring body-level safety through voice, face, breath, movement, and reliable connection.

exampleSpecs.audience: medical residents learning to read body cues
exampleSpecs.stakes: An intake huddle can treat a flat face as information instead of refusal.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use Darwin's emotional expression work to shift attention toward visible body signals.

exampleSpecs.audience: staff supervisors responding after a conflict
exampleSpecs.stakes: A support attempt may feel like threat if staff crowd the doorway.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Apply Polyvagal Theory by rebuilding social engagement before reflection.

exampleSpecs.audience: counselors sorting discipline from survival arousal
exampleSpecs.stakes: A discipline note can miss the body state behind classroom behavior.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use the autonomic safety ladder to read social engagement, fight-or-flight, and collapse.

exampleSpecs.audience: charge nurses planning a safer handoff
exampleSpecs.stakes: A patient may remain mobilized after danger has passed.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show sympathetic activation and the need for a recovery pathway.

exampleSpecs.audience: recreation coaches using rhythm without pressure
exampleSpecs.stakes: Bodily energy can be invited safely or interpreted as threat.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show play, rhythm, voice, face, and movement as safety cues.

exampleSpecs.audience: HR directors supporting staff after a crisis
exampleSpecs.stakes: A return plan can worsen shame if it treats recovery as private toughness.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Challenge individualistic healing by naming co-regulation and social safety.
